title: CSS
intro: CSS styles and lays out HTML. Learn how stylesheets work, then build up through the box model, Flexbox, Grid, responsive design, and modern features — with live examples throughout.

subsections.title: CSS Fundamentals
subsections.description: What CSS is and how styles attach to HTML.

topics.summary: Cascading Style Sheets describe how HTML should look and be laid out.
topics.description: CSS controls colors, fonts, spacing, layout, animation, and responsive behavior. HTML says what something is; CSS says how it should appear. Cascading means multiple rules can apply, and the browser resolves conflicts using specificity and source order. Learning CSS is mostly learning which properties to change and how selectors pick the right elements.
topics.whenToUse: Whenever you style a web page.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not use CSS as a replacement for semantic HTML structure.
commonMistakes: Trying to fix layout bugs by editing HTML structure instead of understanding the cascade and box model.
beginnerTips: Keep HTML for meaning and CSS for appearance — that split makes both easier to maintain.
Use DevTools to see which rules win when something looks wrong.
topics.title: What CSS is

topics.summary: The browser matches selectors to elements, then applies declarations.
topics.description: For each rule, the selector chooses elements (the targets). Declarations inside { } assign properties to values. Cascade, specificity, and inheritance decide the final computed style. If a style does not apply, check whether the selector matched, whether another rule overrode it, or whether the property was inherited.
topics.whenToUse: Debugging unexpected styles or learning why a rule did or did not apply.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not guess overrides — inspect the computed style and the winning rule in DevTools.
commonMistakes: Assuming a rule failed because CSS is broken when the selector simply did not match.
beginnerTips: The Computed panel shows the final values after cascade and inheritance.
Strike-through rules in DevTools mean a more specific or later rule won.
topics.title: How CSS works

topics.summary: style="…" on an element — highest author specificity, hard to maintain.
topics.description: Inline styles apply to one element via the style attribute. They beat most stylesheet rules, which makes them hard to override later. Useful for quick tests, email HTML, or values generated by a script. Prefer classes in a stylesheet for anything you will reuse or maintain.
topics.whenToUse: Tiny one-off overrides, email templates, or dynamically set values from JavaScript.
topics.whenNotToUse: Site-wide styling systems or anything you expect to reuse across elements.
commonMistakes: Building a whole page with inline styles, then struggling to keep colors and spacing consistent.
beginnerTips: If you need an override that feels “stuck,” check for an inline style first.
topics.title: Inline CSS

topics.summary: A <style> block in the document head.
topics.description: Internal CSS keeps rules in a <style> block, usually in the document head. Fine for single-page demos, CodePens, or tiny prototypes. Multi-page sites benefit from shared external files so you do not copy the same rules into every HTML file.
topics.whenToUse: Prototypes, tutorials, and single-file examples.
topics.whenNotToUse: Large multi-page projects that need shared, cacheable styles.
commonMistakes: Duplicating the same <style> block across many pages instead of linking one stylesheet.
beginnerTips: Put <style> in the head so styles load before the body paints when possible.
topics.title: Internal CSS

topics.summary: A .css file linked from the head — the standard approach.
topics.description: Use <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css"> in the head. External files can be cached by the browser, shared across pages, and edited without touching HTML. This is the default setup for almost every real website.
topics.whenToUse: Almost all real websites and multi-page projects.
topics.whenNotToUse: Only skip this for throwaway single-file demos where a <style> block is simpler.
commonMistakes: Linking with the wrong path (missing ./ or wrong folder) so the CSS never loads.
beginnerTips: If styles “do nothing,” check the href path and the Network tab for a 404.
One shared stylesheet (or a small set of them) beats copying rules per page.
topics.title: External CSS

topics.description: A rule set has a selector and a declaration block. Each declaration is property: value; and should end with a semicolon. Comments use /* */ — there are no // comments in standard CSS. Missing braces or semicolons often break the following rules, not just the one you edited.
topics.whenToUse: Writing or reading any stylesheet.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not invent property names; unknown properties are ignored silently.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the semicolon so the next property is parsed incorrectly.
beginnerTips: When a whole chunk of CSS stops working, look for a missing } above the broken part.
topics.title: CSS syntax

topics.summary: Patterns that choose which elements a rule affects.
topics.description: Selectors range from simple (p, .class, #id) to combinators and pseudo-classes. Precise selectors reduce unwanted styling; overly deep selectors become brittle when HTML changes. Prefer a clear class on the element you mean to style over long descendant chains.
topics.whenToUse: Every CSS rule needs a selector that targets the right elements.
topics.whenNotToUse: Extremely long selector chains when a single class would do.
commonMistakes: Writing fragile selectors like div div span that break when the markup shifts slightly.
beginnerTips: Start with a class when you need reuse and control; use element selectors for broad defaults.
topics.title: Selectors (intro)

topics.summary: Properties are the settings; values are what you set them to.
topics.description: color, margin, display, and font-size are properties. Values can be keywords (block), numbers with units (16px, 1.2rem), functions (rgb(), calc()), or custom properties. If a value is invalid for that property, the browser ignores the declaration and keeps the previous value.
topics.whenToUse: All styling — every declaration pairs a property with a value.
topics.whenNotToUse: Inventing unknown property names or mixing incompatible value types.
commonMistakes: Writing color: 16px or width: blue — wrong value types fail silently.
beginnerTips: When nothing changes, check spelling and whether the value type matches the property (e.g. color vs length).
topics.title: Properties and values

topics.summary: Declarations live inside rules; stylesheets are lists of rules.
topics.description: Multiple declarations can share one selector. Multiple selectors can share one block with commas. Order and specificity resolve conflicts when two rules set the same property. Grouping related declarations keeps stylesheets readable.
topics.whenToUse: Organizing stylesheets and sharing declarations across selectors.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not cram unrelated selectors into one comma list just to save lines.
commonMistakes: Assuming the last rule in the file always wins — specificity can beat source order.
beginnerTips: Put the most important or most overridden properties where you can find them quickly.
topics.title: Declarations and rules

topics.summary: /* comment */ — there are no // comments in standard CSS.
topics.description: Comments document intent or temporarily disable rules while debugging. They do not affect layout. Remove large commented dead code when you are done so the file stays trustworthy.
topics.whenToUse: Section labels, short notes, and temporary debugging.
topics.whenNotToUse: Leaving huge commented blocks forever as a substitute for version control.
commonMistakes: Using // comments — they are invalid in standard CSS and can break the next rule.
beginnerTips: Use comments to mark major sections (buttons, layout, utilities) in long files.
topics.title: CSS comments

topics.summary: Target all elements of a tag name.
topics.description: An element selector like p matches every paragraph on the page. Specificity is low, so classes and IDs override them easily. Use element selectors for broad defaults (body font, heading scale), then refine with classes.
topics.whenToUse: Base typography and defaults that should apply to every matching tag.
topics.whenNotToUse: Styling one special paragraph — use a class instead so you do not restyle the whole page.
commonMistakes: Styling div or span globally and accidentally restyling layout wrappers everywhere.
beginnerTips: Good for resets and defaults; pair with classes for component styles.
topics.title: Element selectors

topics.summary: Target elements with a class attribute.
topics.description: A class selector like .note matches any element with class="note". Classes are reusable, readable, and the workhorse of most CSS. One element can have multiple classes; one class can style many elements.
topics.whenToUse: Almost all component and utility styling in real projects.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not invent a new class for every one-off tweak if a small variation of an existing class works.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the dot — note { } is an element selector, not a class.
beginnerTips: Name classes by role or look (.card, .btn-primary), not by exact color (.blue-box).
topics.title: Class selectors

topics.summary: Target one unique id — high specificity.
topics.description: An ID selector like #hero matches the element with that id. IDs are unique in the page and have high specificity, which makes overrides painful. Prefer classes for styling systems; reserve IDs for page anchors or JS hooks when needed.
topics.whenToUse: Rare one-off targets, fragment links, or when an ID already exists for scripting.
topics.whenNotToUse: Reusable UI patterns — classes scale better and are easier to override.
commonMistakes: Using IDs for all styling and then fighting specificity wars with !important.
beginnerTips: If you need !important to beat an ID, switch the style to a class instead.
topics.title: ID selectors

topics.description: The universal selector * matches every element. Common in box-sizing resets or as part of a limited pattern like .card *. Overusing * for heavy styling can make intent unclear and surprise you with nested matches.
topics.whenToUse: Limited resets (e.g. box-sizing) or quick debugging outlines.
topics.whenNotToUse: Painting complex visual styles on every element in a large tree.
commonMistakes: Using * with margin/padding resets without checking form controls and lists.
beginnerTips: Prefer * { box-sizing: border-box; } style resets over styling everything with *.
topics.title: Universal selector

topics.summary: Match elements by attribute presence or value.
topics.description: Attribute selectors match on attributes: [required], [type="email"], [href^="https"]. They are powerful for forms and links without extra classes. Keep them readable — complex attribute chains can be hard to debug.
topics.whenToUse: Styling inputs, links, or data attributes by their HTML attributes.
topics.whenNotToUse: When a shared class is clearer and the attribute is not meaningful to the style.
commonMistakes: Forgetting quotes around values that need them, or matching the wrong attribute name.
beginnerTips: ^= starts with, $= ends with, *= contains — handy for href patterns.
topics.title: Attribute selectors

topics.summary: A B matches B anywhere inside A.
topics.description: A space combinator means descendant: article p styles every paragraph inside article, no matter how deep. Convenient for scoped sections, but easy to over-reach into nested components. Prefer a direct child or a class when nesting depth matters.
topics.whenToUse: Styling content inside a known region without tagging every child.
topics.whenNotToUse: Deeply nested UI where you might style nested cards or lists by accident.
commonMistakes: Writing .nav a and unintentionally styling links inside dropdowns you forgot about.
beginnerTips: If nested content looks wrong, check for a broad descendant rule higher up.
topics.title: Descendant selectors

topics.summary: A > B matches only direct children.
topics.description: The > combinator matches only direct children, not deeper descendants. Use it when nesting depth matters — for example, styling only top-level list items, not nested ones. Narrower than a descendant selector and usually safer for menus and outlines.
topics.whenToUse: When only immediate children should match, such as top-level nav items.
topics.whenNotToUse: When you truly need every nested match — use a descendant selector instead.
commonMistakes: Expecting > to match grandchildren — it only matches one level down.
beginnerTips: Reach for > when a space combinator is styling nested items you did not intend.
topics.title: Child selectors

topics.summary: A + B matches B immediately after A.
topics.description: A + B selects B only when it is the next sibling after A. Classic use: style the first paragraph after a heading. It does not match later siblings — use ~ for that.
topics.whenToUse: Spacing or styling based on the element that comes immediately before.
topics.whenNotToUse: When any following sibling should match — use the general sibling combinator.
commonMistakes: Assuming + matches all following siblings; only the next one counts.
beginnerTips: Great for “label + input” or “heading + first paragraph” patterns.
topics.title: Adjacent sibling

topics.summary: A ~ B matches later siblings of A.
topics.description: A ~ B matches every B that follows A as a sibling (same parent), not only the next one. Useful for pure-CSS patterns with checkboxes and for styling everything after a heading. Order in the HTML still matters — earlier siblings are never matched.
topics.whenToUse: Styling all following siblings, or checkbox/radio sibling tricks.
topics.whenNotToUse: When only the immediate next sibling should change — use + instead.
commonMistakes: Expecting ~ to style nested descendants; it only selects siblings.
beginnerTips: Remember both elements must share the same parent.
topics.title: General sibling

topics.summary: Share a rule across selectors with commas.
topics.description: Comma-separated selectors share one declaration block: h1, h2, h3 { }. This avoids copying the same declarations. Keep the group coherent — if one selector later needs different styles, split it out.
topics.whenToUse: Shared styles across related elements or components.
topics.whenNotToUse: Grouping unrelated selectors that will soon need different values.
commonMistakes: Leaving a trailing comma before the { which invalidates the rule in some cases.
beginnerTips: Put each selector on its own line in long lists for easier diffs and reading.
topics.title: Multiple selectors

subsections.title: Colors
subsections.description: Ways to specify color and transparency.

topics.description: Named colors are easy keywords such as red, steelblue, or transparent. Fine for demos and quick sketches. Design systems usually prefer a limited palette stored as variables so brand colors stay consistent.
topics.whenToUse: Quick prototypes, teaching demos, or transparent / currentColor.
topics.whenNotToUse: Brand palettes in production — named colors are hard to keep consistent.
commonMistakes: Mixing many random named colors instead of a small intentional palette.
beginnerTips: currentColor is useful so borders and icons follow the text color.
topics.title: Named colors

topics.description: Hex notation is common in design tools: #2563eb is a vivid blue. Short form #rgb expands each digit (#f00 → #ff0000). Eight-digit hex adds alpha. Copy hex values from Figma or similar and paste them into CSS.
topics.whenToUse: Matching colors from design tools and brand guidelines.
topics.whenNotToUse: When you need to tweak lightness often — HSL is often easier for that.
commonMistakes: Writing #2563eb0.5 — alpha belongs in #rrggbbaa or a separate opacity/alpha channel.
beginnerTips: Store hex tokens in CSS variables so you change a color in one place.
topics.title: HEX colors

topics.description: RGB matches how screens mix light: three channels from 0–255. Modern CSS also accepts rgb(37 99 235) with spaces. Use RGB when you already think in channel values or when converting from other tools.
topics.whenToUse: When working with channel values from code or graphics tools.
topics.whenNotToUse: Hand-tuning shades by eye — HSL is usually more intuitive for that.
commonMistakes: Using values outside 0–255 or mixing percent and number forms incorrectly.
beginnerTips: Same color as #2563eb: rgb(37, 99, 235).
topics.title: RGB

topics.description: RGBA adds an alpha channel: 0 is fully transparent, 1 is opaque. Unlike opacity on an element, color alpha only affects that color — child text can stay fully opaque. Prefer modern rgb(… / 0.45) syntax when you can.
topics.whenToUse: Overlays, translucent backgrounds, and soft borders without fading children.
topics.whenNotToUse: Fading an entire component including its text — use opacity (carefully) instead.
commonMistakes: Using opacity on a parent when you only meant to fade the background color.
beginnerTips: Use translucent backgrounds over solid page colors for layered UI.
topics.title: RGBA

topics.summary: Hue, saturation, lightness — intuitive for adjusting shades.
topics.description: HSL describes color as hue (0–360), saturation, and lightness. Change lightness to get tints and shades without hunting new hex values. Great for generating palettes and dark/light variants programmatically.
topics.whenToUse: Building related shades, themes, and adjustable palettes.
topics.whenNotToUse: When a designer already handed you exact hex tokens and you do not need to derive variants.
commonMistakes: Confusing saturation with lightness — both change how strong the color looks.
beginnerTips: Keep hue fixed and vary lightness for a simple monochrome scale.
topics.title: HSL

topics.description: HSLA is HSL plus transparency. Modern syntax writes alpha after a slash: hsl(217 91% 60% / 0.5). Same benefits as HSL for tuning hue, with alpha for overlays.
topics.whenToUse: Translucent theme colors when you already work in HSL.
topics.whenNotToUse: When you only need a solid color — skip the alpha channel.
commonMistakes: Mixing old hsla() commas with modern slash syntax incorrectly.
beginnerTips: Match hue to your solid brand color, then lower alpha for overlays.
topics.title: HSLA

topics.description: opacity fades the entire element, including text and children. Color alpha (rgba/hsla/hex alpha) fades only that paint. Choose based on whether children should stay crisp. Stacking translucent layers also compounds visually.
topics.whenToUse: opacity for whole-element fade effects; color alpha for backgrounds and borders.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not use opacity on a wrapper when you only wanted a see-through background.
commonMistakes: Putting opacity on a parent and wondering why child text looks washed out.
beginnerTips: Disabled UI often uses opacity; overlays usually use background alpha.
topics.title: Transparency

topics.description: linear-gradient and radial-gradient create smooth color blends without image files. They are treated as background images. Use them for heroes, buttons, and decorative depth — keep contrast readable when text sits on top.
topics.whenToUse: Decorative backgrounds, buttons, and soft depth without exporting images.
topics.whenNotToUse: Photographic imagery — use a real image for that.
commonMistakes: Placing light text on a mid-gradient without checking contrast at every stop.
beginnerTips: List the direction first (e.g. 135deg or to right), then color stops.
topics.title: Gradients

topics.description: The color property sets the foreground color of text and, via currentColor, can influence borders and icons. It inherits to children by default, so setting color on a parent often styles nested text too. Always check contrast against the background.
topics.whenToUse: Setting readable text and link colors.
topics.whenNotToUse: Coloring non-text boxes — use background-color for fills.
commonMistakes: Low-contrast text (light gray on white) that fails accessibility checks.
beginnerTips: Inherit is the default; you rarely need to set color on every child.
topics.title: color

topics.description: font-family lists preferred fonts, ending with a generic family like sans-serif or serif. If the first font is missing, the browser tries the next. Quote multi-word names. Web fonts need a @font-face or a link before they appear in the stack.
topics.whenToUse: Setting brand typefaces and reliable fallbacks.
topics.whenNotToUse: Listing only an obscure font with no fallback — missing fonts look broken.
commonMistakes: Forgetting quotes around 'Times New Roman' and breaking the stack.
beginnerTips: Always end stacks with a generic family: serif, sans-serif, monospace.
topics.title: font-family

topics.description: font-size accepts px, rem, em, and fluid functions like clamp(). rem scales with the root size and is predictable for design systems. em scales with the parent font size, which can compound in nested elements.
topics.whenToUse: Setting body, heading, and UI text sizes.
topics.whenNotToUse: Tiny fixed px sizes that ignore user zoom preferences — prefer rem for body text.
commonMistakes: Nesting em sizes so text becomes unexpectedly huge or tiny.
beginnerTips: Body text around 1rem with rem-based headings keeps the scale coherent.
topics.title: font-size

topics.description: font-weight controls boldness with keywords or numeric weights (100–900). The font file must include that weight — otherwise the browser may fake bold poorly. Load the weights you use when working with web fonts.
topics.whenToUse: Emphasizing headings, labels, and strong UI text.
topics.whenNotToUse: Faking bold when the typeface has no bold face loaded — load the real weight.
commonMistakes: Requesting font-weight: 600 without loading a 600 file, getting ugly synthetic bold.
beginnerTips: 400 is normal, 700 is bold in most numeric scales.
topics.title: font-weight

topics.description: font-style: italic requests an italic face; oblique is a slanted synthetic style. If no italic face exists, the browser may synthesize one. Prefer a real italic cut from the font family when available.
topics.whenToUse: Emphasis, quotes, and editorial accents.
topics.whenNotToUse: Long body paragraphs entirely in italic — harder to read.
commonMistakes: Assuming every font has a true italic — many UI fonts only have upright.
beginnerTips: Use <em> for stressed emphasis and style it if needed; do not rely on italics alone for meaning.
topics.title: font-style

topics.description: text-align aligns inline content inside a block: left, right, center, or justify. It does not center a block box itself — use margin: auto or flex/grid for that. Inherited by children.
topics.whenToUse: Aligning paragraph text, headings, and table cell text.
topics.whenNotToUse: Centering a whole card or layout column — that is a layout job, not text-align alone.
commonMistakes: Using text-align: center on a wrapper expecting the box to center in the viewport.
beginnerTips: Center short headings; keep long body copy left-aligned for readability.
topics.title: text-align

topics.description: text-decoration draws lines such as underline or line-through. Links are underlined by default in many browsers — removing underlines needs a clear hover/focus affordance. You can also set decoration color and thickness in modern CSS.
topics.whenToUse: Link affordances, delete markup, and subtle emphasis lines.
topics.whenNotToUse: Removing link underlines without another clear interactive cue.
commonMistakes: Stripping underlines from links so they look like plain text.
beginnerTips: Pair text-decoration: none on links with a distinct color and :hover/:focus styles.
topics.title: text-decoration

topics.description: text-transform changes visual casing without editing the HTML. Screen readers still use the underlying text. Useful for small labels and headings; avoid shouting entire paragraphs in uppercase.
topics.whenToUse: UI labels, eyebrow text, and stylized headings.
topics.whenNotToUse: Long reading content — all caps slows reading.
commonMistakes: Typing uppercase in HTML and also applying text-transform, making edits awkward.
beginnerTips: Add a little letter-spacing when using uppercase for balance.
topics.title: text-transform

topics.description: line-height controls the height of each line of text. Unitless values like 1.5 scale cleanly with font-size. Too tight feels cramped; too loose looks sparse. Body copy often sits around 1.5–1.7.
topics.whenToUse: Improving readability of paragraphs and UI text blocks.
topics.whenNotToUse: Using huge line-height to create vertical layout gaps — prefer margin/gap.

files.code: Line height controls how comfortable paragraphs feel when text wraps across multiple lines.

commonMistakes: Setting line-height in px and then changing font-size, breaking the rhythm.
beginnerTips: Prefer unitless line-height so nested sizes stay proportional.
topics.title: line-height

topics.description: letter-spacing (tracking) adjusts space between characters. Slight positive tracking can help uppercase headings. Large spacing hurts readability for body text. Negative values tighten glyphs for display type carefully.
topics.whenToUse: Polishing headings, logos, and small caps-style labels.
topics.whenNotToUse: Body paragraphs — extra tracking makes reading harder.
commonMistakes: Cranking letter-spacing so words no longer read as words.
beginnerTips: Start with small values like 0.02em–0.08em and adjust by eye.
topics.title: letter-spacing

topics.description: word-spacing adjusts the gap between words. Use sparingly — browsers already handle normal spacing well. Large values look broken; tiny tweaks sometimes help justified text or stylized headings.
topics.whenToUse: Rare typographic fine-tuning.
topics.whenNotToUse: Everyday layout spacing — use margin, gap, or padding instead.
commonMistakes: Using word-spacing as a substitute for padding between UI items.
beginnerTips: If words look uneven, check justification and font before word-spacing.
topics.title: word-spacing

topics.description: text-shadow draws a shadow behind glyphs: offset-x offset-y blur color. Keep it subtle so text stays readable. Multiple shadows are allowed, but heavy stacks look dated and can hurt contrast.
topics.whenToUse: Light emphasis on headings over busy backgrounds.
topics.whenNotToUse: Body text or anything that needs crisp accessibility contrast.
commonMistakes: Huge bright shadows that make letters fuzzy and hard to read.
beginnerTips: A soft dark shadow can help white text sit on a photo — still verify contrast.
topics.title: text-shadow

topics.description: Combine white-space, overflow, and text-overflow: ellipsis for single-line truncation. Wrapping controls whether long words break. Truncation hides content, so make sure users can still access the full text when it matters.
topics.whenToUse: Single-line labels, table cells, and cards with limited width.
topics.whenNotToUse: Critical content users must read in full without another way to see it.

files.code: This is a very long line that will truncate with an ellipsis when too wide.

commonMistakes: Setting only text-overflow: ellipsis without overflow and nowrap — nothing truncates.
beginnerTips: Ellipsis needs a constrained width plus overflow: hidden and white-space: nowrap.
topics.title: Overflow & wrapping

topics.summary: Every element is a rectangular box with content + padding + border + margin.
topics.description: Content is the inner area. Padding is space inside the border. Border wraps the padding. Margin is space outside the border separating from others. Most layout bugs are box-model bugs: unexpected width, collapsed margins, or padding added on top of width. DevTools box model diagram makes these layers visible.
topics.whenToUse: Debugging size, spacing, and why an element is larger than its width suggests.
topics.whenNotToUse: Do not ignore the box model when using Flexbox or Grid — items are still boxes.
commonMistakes: Setting width: 100% plus padding and wondering why the box overflows its parent.
beginnerTips: Click an element in DevTools and study the box-model graphic (content/padding/border/margin).
Remember: default content-box means padding and border add to width.
topics.title: Box model overview

topics.description: width and height size the content box by default (content-box). Percentage widths are relative to the parent’s width. Height percentages only work if the parent has a defined height. Prefer min-height over fixed height for content that can grow.
topics.whenToUse: Setting explicit sizes for boxes, media frames, and layout tracks.
topics.whenNotToUse: Locking height on text containers that need to grow with content.
commonMistakes: Using height: 100% without a parent height chain, so nothing happens.
beginnerTips: For fluid layouts, prefer max-width and min-height over rigid width/height pairs.
topics.title: width & height

topics.summary: min-width, max-width, min-height, max-height constrain growth.
topics.description: min- and max- size properties constrain how far a box can shrink or grow. max-width: 100% keeps images from overflowing. min-height helps empty states and cards keep a usable size without clipping content when it grows.
topics.whenToUse: Responsive images, readable measure (max-width on text), and flexible cards.
topics.whenNotToUse: Fighting Flexbox/Grid with conflicting min-width when the layout already controls size.
commonMistakes: Setting both width and max-width in conflicting ways without checking the result.
beginnerTips: max-width on paragraphs (e.g. 40rem) improves line length for reading.
topics.title: min/max size

topics.summary: Outer spacing; can collapse vertically between blocks.
topics.description: Margin is space outside the border. Vertical margins between block elements can collapse into one shared gap. Horizontal margin: auto centers a block that has a width. Margin does not include background color of the element.
topics.whenToUse: Separating elements from each other and centering block boxes.
topics.whenNotToUse: Inner spacing inside a box — that is padding.
commonMistakes: Surprise spacing from vertical margin collapse between stacked blocks.
beginnerTips: In flex/grid containers, prefer gap over margins between items.
topics.title: margin

topics.summary: Inner spacing between content and border.
topics.description: Padding sits between content and border and shares the element’s background. It increases clickable area for buttons and makes text less cramped in cards. Padding adds to total size unless you use box-sizing: border-box.
topics.whenToUse: Breathing room inside buttons, cards, inputs, and content boxes.
topics.whenNotToUse: Separating two sibling elements — use margin or gap.
commonMistakes: Using padding to push siblings apart and then fighting background bleed.
beginnerTips: Symmetric padding (e.g. 0.5rem 1rem) is common for buttons: vertical then horizontal.
topics.title: padding

topics.summary: Width, style, and color of the border.
topics.description: Borders need width, style, and color — shorthand border: 1px solid #000 sets all three. Style is required; without it you may see no border. Borders affect layout size under content-box sizing.
topics.whenToUse: Outlining cards, inputs, dividers, and focusable regions.
topics.whenNotToUse: Focus rings that should not affect layout — consider outline instead.
commonMistakes: Setting only border-width and border-color without border-style — nothing shows.
beginnerTips: Shorthand order people remember: width style color.
topics.title: border

topics.summary: Include padding/border in width calculations with border-box.
topics.description: With content-box (default), width is content only — padding and border add outside it. With border-box, width includes padding and border, which matches how most people sketch UI. Many resets set * { box-sizing: border-box; }.
topics.whenToUse: Almost every modern layout — especially width: 100% with padding.
topics.whenNotToUse: Rare cases where you intentionally want padding to expand past the set width.
commonMistakes: Mixing box-sizing models across components and getting inconsistent widths.
beginnerTips: Set border-box once globally early in the stylesheet.
topics.title: box-sizing

topics.description: Colored layers make padding versus outer spacing easier to see. Backgrounds paint through padding but not margin. Use this mental model when spacing looks wrong: is the gap inside the border or outside it?
topics.whenToUse: Learning and teaching the difference between padding and margin.
topics.whenNotToUse: Production styling — temporary debug backgrounds should be removed.
commonMistakes: Assuming margin is “inside” the colored area — margin is outside the border.
beginnerTips: Temporarily add background colors while debugging spacing.
topics.title: Visual box model demo

subsections.title: Display
subsections.description: How elements generate boxes and participate in layout.

topics.summary: Starts on a new line; stretches to available width.
topics.description: Block boxes start on a new line and stretch to the available width by default. Headings, paragraphs, and divs are block-level. You can set width/height and vertical margins more freely than with inline boxes.
topics.whenToUse: Stacking sections, full-width containers, and forcing a new line.
topics.whenNotToUse: Words inside a sentence that should flow with text — keep those inline.
commonMistakes: Wrapping every word in a block and breaking natural text flow.
beginnerTips: A span becomes a full-width stack item when you set display: block.
topics.title: display: block

topics.description: Inline boxes flow with text like words in a sentence. Width and height generally do not apply; top/bottom margins do not behave like block margins. Links and <em> are inline by default. Padding can still show horizontally.
topics.whenToUse: Styling pieces of text that must stay in the reading flow.
topics.whenNotToUse: Sizing chips, buttons, or cards — use inline-block, flex, or block.
commonMistakes: Setting width on an inline element and wondering why nothing changes.
beginnerTips: If width/height seem ignored, check whether the element is still inline.
topics.title: display: inline

topics.summary: Flows like inline but accepts width/height.
topics.description: inline-block flows with text like inline but accepts width, height, and vertical padding more like a block. Useful for nav items, tags, and button-like controls sitting in a row. Whitespace between tags can create small gaps.
topics.whenToUse: Horizontal items that need explicit size without full flex/grid.
topics.whenNotToUse: Complex alignment or equal-height rows — Flexbox is usually clearer.
commonMistakes: Fighting inline-block gaps for a whole navbar instead of using flex + gap.
beginnerTips: Mysterious gaps are often HTML whitespace between inline-block siblings.
topics.title: display: inline-block

topics.summary: Removes the element from layout entirely.
topics.description: display: none removes the element from layout as if it were not there — no space reserved. visibility: hidden hides it but still occupies space. For accessibility, hiding from everyone is different from visually hiding but keeping for screen readers.
topics.whenToUse: Completely removing UI from layout (tabs, collapsed panels, unused markup).
topics.whenNotToUse: Temporary hide when you still need the space reserved — use visibility or opacity.
commonMistakes: Using display: none for content that should remain available to assistive tech without a proper pattern.
beginnerTips: Toggling display with JS remounts layout; transitions cannot animate to none smoothly.
topics.title: display: none

topics.summary: Turns children into flex items for one-dimensional layout.
topics.description: display: flex creates a flex formatting context: children become flex items arranged on one main axis (row or column). Great for nav bars, toolbars, and equal-height cards in a row. See the Flexbox section for alignment, grow, and wrap details.
topics.whenToUse: One-dimensional rows or columns with alignment and distribution control.
topics.whenNotToUse: Full two-dimensional page grids — start with CSS Grid instead.
commonMistakes: Nesting flex for everything when a simple block stack would do.
beginnerTips: Add gap for spacing between items instead of margins on every child.
topics.title: display: flex (intro)

topics.summary: Two-dimensional layout of rows and columns.
topics.description: display: grid creates rows and columns at once. Children become grid items placed into cells. Ideal for page shells, card galleries, and overlapping controlled areas. See the Grid section for tracks, areas, and responsive auto-fit patterns.
topics.whenToUse: Layouts that need both rows and columns defined together.
topics.whenNotToUse: Simple single-row toolbars — Flexbox is often enough.
commonMistakes: Using Grid only to center one item when flex or margin: auto is simpler.
beginnerTips: Define columns with grid-template-columns first; rows can often auto-size.
topics.title: display: grid (intro)

topics.description: static is the default position. Elements sit in normal document flow, and inset properties (top, left, right, bottom) have no effect. z-index also does not apply to static boxes in the classic model. You rarely set static unless resetting a previous position.
topics.whenToUse: Normal flow layout — the default for nearly every element.
topics.whenNotToUse: When you need offsets, sticky headers, or overlapping layers.
commonMistakes: Setting top without changing position, then thinking CSS is broken.
beginnerTips: If top/left do nothing, the element is probably still position: static.
topics.title: position: static

topics.summary: Offset from its normal position; still occupies original space.
topics.description: relative offsets an element visually with top/left/right/bottom while keeping its original space in normal flow. Commonly used as a positioning context for absolute children. Small nudges are fine; large offsets can confuse layout.
topics.whenToUse: Anchoring absolute children, or small visual nudges without removing flow space.
topics.whenNotToUse: Major page layout — prefer flex, grid, or margin for structure.
commonMistakes: Using relative offsets to build whole layouts that break when content changes.
beginnerTips: Put position: relative on the parent before using absolute on a child.
topics.title: position: relative

topics.summary: Positioned relative to the nearest positioned ancestor.
topics.description: absolute removes the element from normal flow and positions it against the nearest ancestor with position other than static (or the viewport). Siblings do not reserve space for it. Great for badges, close buttons, and overlays inside a relative parent.
topics.whenToUse: Overlays, icons, and controls pinned inside a positioned parent.
topics.whenNotToUse: General document flow — absolute elements do not push siblings down.
commonMistakes: Forgetting position: relative on the parent and watching the child jump to the wrong ancestor.
beginnerTips: Always set a positioned parent; otherwise the abs element may anchor to a higher box.
topics.title: position: absolute

topics.summary: Fixed to the viewport — stays while scrolling.
topics.description: fixed pins an element to the viewport so it stays put while the page scrolls. Used for floating actions and persistent bars. transform or filter on an ancestor can create a new containing block and change what “viewport” means.
topics.whenToUse: UI that must remain visible while the page scrolls (within the viewport).
topics.whenNotToUse: In-section headers that should stick inside a container — use sticky.
commonMistakes: Covering important content with a fixed bar without adding body padding.
beginnerTips: Check mobile safe areas and overlapping content under fixed bars.
topics.title: position: fixed

topics.summary: Acts relative until a scroll threshold, then sticks.
topics.description: sticky behaves like relative until a threshold (e.g. top: 0), then sticks within its containing scroll area. The parent must have room to scroll; overflow: hidden on ancestors often breaks sticky. Great for table headers and section labels.
topics.whenToUse: Headers and labels that stick while their section scrolls.
topics.whenNotToUse: Elements that must stay fixed to the viewport even outside their parent — use fixed.
commonMistakes: An ancestor with overflow: hidden quietly disabling sticky behavior.
beginnerTips: You need a threshold like top: 0; sticky without an inset does little.
topics.title: position: sticky

topics.summary: Controls stacking order among positioned elements.
topics.description: z-index controls stacking among positioned elements (and flex/grid items in modern rules). Higher values paint on top. New stacking contexts (opacity < 1, transform, etc.) can isolate z-index so a huge number still loses to another context.
topics.whenToUse: Overlapping UI: dropdowns, modals, tooltips, badges.
topics.whenNotToUse: Normal non-overlapping flow — you usually do not need z-index.
commonMistakes: Setting z-index on a static element and expecting it to rise above others.
beginnerTips: Keep a small scale (e.g. 1, 10, 100) instead of random 9999 wars.
topics.title: z-index & stacking

subsections.title: Flexbox
subsections.description: One-dimensional layout: rows or columns with alignment control.

topics.summary: Enables flex formatting context on the container.
topics.description: Setting display: flex on a container makes its children flex items. The container controls direction, wrapping, and alignment. Start here, then add justify-content, align-items, and gap as needed.
topics.whenToUse: Any one-axis layout: nav, toolbars, form rows, card rows.
topics.whenNotToUse: True 2D page templates with rows and columns defined together — use Grid.
commonMistakes: Putting display: flex on every child instead of the container.
beginnerTips: Apply flex to the parent; children become items automatically.
topics.title: display: flex

topics.description: flex-direction sets the main axis: row (default) or column, plus reverse variants. justify-content works along the main axis; align-items works on the cross axis. Changing direction swaps which axis those properties affect.
topics.whenToUse: Switching between horizontal and vertical stacks.
topics.whenNotToUse: Reordering for visual preference when HTML source order is better for accessibility — prefer editing markup when you can.
commonMistakes: Tweaking align-items when you meant justify-content after changing direction.
beginnerTips: In column direction, justify-content controls vertical distribution.
topics.title: flex-direction

topics.summary: Aligns items along the main axis.
topics.description: justify-content distributes free space along the main axis: flex-start, center, space-between, space-around, space-evenly, and more. It does not size the items themselves — flex-grow and width do that.
topics.whenToUse: Spreading or centering items along the row or column main axis.
topics.whenNotToUse: Aligning on the cross axis — that is align-items.
commonMistakes: Expecting justify-content to wrap items — use flex-wrap for that.
beginnerTips: space-between puts the first and last items flush with the edges.
topics.title: justify-content

topics.summary: Aligns items on the cross axis.
topics.description: align-items aligns items on the cross axis (vertical in a row). stretch is the default and makes items fill the container’s cross size when heights are auto. center is the classic vertical centering trick in a flex row.
topics.whenToUse: Vertical alignment in a row, or horizontal alignment in a column.
topics.whenNotToUse: Distributing space along the main axis — use justify-content.
commonMistakes: Wondering why align-items: center does nothing when the container is only as tall as its items.
beginnerTips: Give the flex container a height if you want visible cross-axis centering.
topics.title: align-items

topics.description: align-content packs multiple flex lines when items wrap and there is extra cross-axis space. It does nothing for a single line. If you meant to align items inside one line, use align-items instead.
topics.whenToUse: Multi-line flex containers with leftover vertical (or cross-axis) space.
topics.whenNotToUse: Single-line flex layouts — align-content will appear to do nothing.
commonMistakes: Confusing align-content with align-items when debugging vertical centering.
beginnerTips: Remember: wrap first, then align-content can take effect.
topics.title: align-content

topics.summary: Allow items to wrap to new lines.
topics.description: nowrap (default) keeps items on one line, which can cause overflow. wrap lets items flow onto new lines when space runs out. Pair with flex-basis or min widths for responsive chip/row layouts.
topics.whenToUse: Responsive rows of cards, tags, or buttons that should reflow.
topics.whenNotToUse: When items must stay on one line and shrink instead — keep nowrap and control flex-shrink.
commonMistakes: Forcing nowrap and horizontal scroll when wrapping would be clearer on small screens.
beginnerTips: Combine wrap with gap so new lines keep even spacing.
topics.title: flex-wrap

topics.summary: Spacing between flex/grid items without margin hacks.
topics.description: gap sets gutters between flex or grid items without margin collapsing tricks. row-gap and column-gap control each axis. Gap only spaces between items, not outside the group — use padding on the container for outer inset.
topics.whenToUse: Consistent spacing between siblings in flex or grid containers.
topics.whenNotToUse: Outer page margins — pad the container or margin the group itself.
commonMistakes: Adding both large margins and gap, doubling the intended space.
beginnerTips: Prefer gap over margin-right on every item (and removing it on the last child).
topics.title: gap

topics.description: The flex shorthand sets grow, shrink, and basis together. flex: 1 is a common equal-width pattern (items share space). Prefer the shorthand over setting the three longhands inconsistently.
topics.whenToUse: Equal-width columns and flexible items that share free space.
topics.whenNotToUse: Fixed-size icons or buttons that should not grow — leave flex at initial/auto.
commonMistakes: Setting only flex-grow and forgetting basis, getting uneven starting sizes.
beginnerTips: flex: 1 1 auto and flex: 1 are common; learn what your reset defaults to.
topics.title: flex shorthand

topics.summary: How leftover main-axis space is distributed.
topics.description: flex-grow is a factor for distributing leftover main-axis space. 0 means do not grow (default). An item with grow 2 takes twice as much free space as one with grow 1. Growth only happens if free space exists.
topics.whenToUse: Letting some items expand to fill unused space.
topics.whenNotToUse: When the container has no free space — grow cannot create room from nothing.
commonMistakes: Expecting grow to shrink overflowing items — that is flex-shrink.
beginnerTips: Compare grow factors as ratios, not absolute pixels.
topics.title: flex-grow

topics.summary: How items shrink when space is tight.
topics.description: flex-shrink controls how items shrink when the main size overflows. Default is 1. Set 0 to prevent shrinking (useful for logos). Content min-size can still stop items from shrinking below their content unless you adjust min-width.
topics.whenToUse: Protecting important items from being crushed, or allowing others to compress.
topics.whenNotToUse: Prefer wrapping or smaller bases when shrinking would make text unreadable.
commonMistakes: Leaving long words unshrinkable and overflowing the flex row.
beginnerTips: min-width: 0 on flex children often allows text truncation to work.
topics.title: flex-shrink

topics.description: flex-basis sets the starting main size before grow/shrink. It can be px, %, or auto. Think of it as the ideal size you start from; grow and shrink adjust from there when space is loose or tight.
topics.whenToUse: Giving items a preferred starting width in a flexible row.
topics.whenNotToUse: When width alone is clearer and you are not using grow/shrink.
commonMistakes: Setting both width and flex-basis without realizing which one wins in your browser/context.
beginnerTips: flex: 1 1 200px means start near 200px, then grow/shrink as needed.
topics.title: flex-basis

topics.description: align-self overrides the container’s align-items for a single item. Useful when one card or icon should sit differently from its siblings. Values match align-items (flex-start, center, stretch, etc.).
topics.whenToUse: One outlier item that needs different cross-axis alignment.
topics.whenNotToUse: Changing every item — set align-items on the container instead.
commonMistakes: Sprinkling align-self everywhere instead of fixing the container default.
beginnerTips: Handy for pinning a badge or action to the bottom of a flex row.
topics.title: align-self

topics.summary: Visual order without changing HTML source order.
topics.description: order changes visual order of flex/grid items without editing HTML. Default is 0. Lower numbers appear earlier. Source order still drives keyboard tabbing and screen reader reading, so do not use order to “fix” accessibility problems.
topics.whenToUse: Small visual reorderings when markup order must stay for semantics or CMS reasons.
topics.whenNotToUse: Major content reordering — change the HTML for accessibility.
commonMistakes: Using order so visual layout and focus order disagree in confusing ways.
beginnerTips: If tab order feels wrong after using order, fix the source order instead.
topics.title: order

topics.summary: Enables grid layout on the container.
topics.description: display: grid turns a container into a grid formatting context. Children become grid items placed into cells formed by rows and columns. Define tracks with template properties, then place or span items as needed.
topics.whenToUse: Two-dimensional layouts: page shells, galleries, dashboards.
topics.whenNotToUse: Simple single-axis toolbars — Flexbox is often enough.
commonMistakes: Forgetting display: grid and setting template columns that do nothing.
beginnerTips: Start with columns; let rows create themselves unless you need fixed row sizes.
topics.title: display: grid

topics.description: grid-template-columns defines vertical tracks. Use lengths, fr units, auto, repeat(), and minmax(). fr shares free space proportionally — 2fr 1fr makes the first column twice as wide as the second.
topics.whenToUse: Declaring how many columns exist and how wide they are.
topics.whenNotToUse: Sizing a single flex row — you may not need Grid columns at all.
commonMistakes: Using % tracks that overflow because gaps were not accounted for — prefer fr + gap.
beginnerTips: 1fr 1fr is equal columns; repeat(3, 1fr) is three equal columns.
topics.title: grid-template-columns

topics.description: grid-template-rows defines horizontal tracks with the same kinds of values as columns. Often you only set columns and let rows size to content. Explicit rows help for equal-height bands or fixed chrome.
topics.whenToUse: Fixed or proportional row heights in a grid layout.
topics.whenNotToUse: When content should dictate row height — leave rows auto.
commonMistakes: Locking rows too short and clipping content unexpectedly.
beginnerTips: auto rows grow with content; fr rows share leftover height when the grid has a height.
topics.title: grid-template-rows

topics.description: gap (and row-gap / column-gap) create gutters between grid tracks without margin hacks. Gaps are not applied outside the outer edges — pad the grid container for outer inset. Works the same idea as flex gap.
topics.whenToUse: Even spacing between grid cells.
topics.whenNotToUse: Page margins around the whole grid — use padding/margin on the container.
commonMistakes: Adding margins on every cell and gap, doubling spacing.
beginnerTips: One gap value sets both axes; two values set row then column.
topics.title: gap (grid)

topics.summary: Span or place an item across columns.
topics.description: grid-column places an item on column lines or spans multiple columns. grid-column: 1 / 3 spans from line 1 to 3. 1 / -1 spans the full width. Line numbers include the outer edges.
topics.whenToUse: Full-width headers inside a multi-column grid, or spanning cards.
topics.whenNotToUse: When named areas would be clearer for a whole page template.
commonMistakes: Off-by-one spans because track count was confused with line count.
beginnerTips: Remember lines, not tracks: three columns have four vertical lines.
topics.title: grid-column

topics.description: grid-row works like grid-column on the vertical axis. Span multiple rows for sidebars that stretch beside stacked content. Combine with column placement for precise positioning.
topics.whenToUse: Tall sidebars or items that should cover multiple row tracks.
topics.whenNotToUse: Simple stacked content — normal flow or a single column may be enough.
commonMistakes: Spanning rows without enough explicit rows defined, getting unexpected auto rows.
beginnerTips: Pair grid-row with grid-column when an item needs an exact cell.
topics.title: grid-row

topics.description: Named areas let you sketch a layout in ASCII with grid-template-areas, then assign items with grid-area. Excellent for page shells (header, main, aside, footer). Keep names short and consistent.
topics.whenToUse: Readable full-page or component region layouts.
topics.whenNotToUse: Tiny two-cell grids where line-based placement is shorter.
commonMistakes: Mismatched area names between the template and grid-area values.
beginnerTips: Each string in template-areas is a row; repeat a name to span columns.
topics.title: grid-area

topics.description: repeat() shortens track lists: repeat(3, 1fr) builds three equal columns. Combine with minmax and auto-fit for responsive grids. Prefer repeat over typing the same track many times.
topics.whenToUse: Equal columns/rows or long repeated track patterns.
topics.whenNotToUse: Highly irregular tracks that are each different — write them out.
commonMistakes: Using a fixed repeat(4, 1fr) on mobile without a media query or auto-fit.
beginnerTips: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(...)) is the responsive cards pattern.
topics.title: repeat()

topics.summary: Set a track’s minimum and maximum size.
topics.description: minmax(min, max) clamps a track between two sizes. minmax(10rem, 1fr) is a classic: columns stay at least 10rem but can grow. Prevents tracks from crushing content or exploding without limit.
topics.whenToUse: Responsive tracks that need a floor and a flexible ceiling.
topics.whenNotToUse: Fixed pixel columns that never flex.
commonMistakes: Setting a min larger than the container so the grid overflows.
beginnerTips: Pair with repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min, 1fr)) for fluid card grids.
topics.title: minmax()

topics.description: auto-fit and auto-fill create as many columns as fit. With minmax, cards wrap automatically as the container shrinks. auto-fit collapses empty tracks so items expand; auto-fill keeps empty tracks. For most card grids, auto-fit is what you want.
topics.whenToUse: Card galleries and dashboards that reflow without many media queries.
topics.whenNotToUse: Strict column counts that must stay fixed at every breakpoint.
commonMistakes: Using a huge minimum (e.g. 400px) so you only ever get one column.
beginnerTips: Tune the minmax minimum until cards feel comfortable on mobile and desktop.
topics.title: auto-fit & auto-fill

topics.description: background-color fills the padding box behind content (transparent by default). It does not paint margin. Use solid colors for surfaces; use images/gradients when you need more visual depth.
topics.whenToUse: Page surfaces, cards, buttons, and section fills.
topics.whenNotToUse: Tinting text — use color for foreground text.
commonMistakes: Expecting background-color to cover margins.
beginnerTips: Background shows through padding; margin stays outside the painted area.
topics.title: Background color

topics.description: background-image draws an image (or gradient) behind content. Decorative imagery belongs in CSS; meaningful photos with content value usually belong in for accessibility and SEO. Control size and position with related properties.
topics.whenToUse: Decorative heroes, patterns, and non-content imagery.
topics.whenNotToUse: Important pictures that need alt text — use an .
commonMistakes: Putting critical information only in a background image so screen readers miss it.
beginnerTips: Set a background-color fallback while images load.
topics.title: Background image

topics.summary: Gradients are images generated by CSS.
topics.description: Gradients are CSS-generated images you can use as backgrounds. Layer multiple backgrounds separated by commas (first listed paints on top). Useful for soft depth without exporting assets.
topics.whenToUse: Decorative depth, buttons, and layered washes.
topics.whenNotToUse: Exact photographic scenes — use a real image file.
commonMistakes: Too many loud gradients competing with text contrast.
beginnerTips: You can layer a radial highlight over a linear base.
topics.title: Background gradients

topics.description: background-size controls scaling (cover, contain, or lengths). background-position anchors the image. cover fills the box and may crop; contain fits the whole image and may letterbox. Pair with no-repeat when you do not want tiling.
topics.whenToUse: Cropping and placing decorative background images in a box.
topics.whenNotToUse: Fine art direction of content photos — prefer with object-fit.
commonMistakes: Using contain when you expected a full-bleed crop (that is cover).
beginnerTips: cover is common for full-bleed hero backgrounds.
topics.title: Position & size

topics.description: background-repeat controls tiling. Patterns often use repeat; photos usually use no-repeat with size/position. You can set different repeat behavior per layered background.
topics.whenToUse: Seamless patterns or disabling tiling on photos.
topics.whenNotToUse: When a single stretched image should fill the box — size/position matter more.
commonMistakes: Leaving repeat on a non-tileable photo and seeing a quilt of copies.
beginnerTips: Default is repeat — set no-repeat explicitly for most UI photos.
topics.title: Background repeat

topics.summary: The three pieces of a border (or shorthand).
topics.description: A visible border needs width, style, and color. Styles include solid, dashed, dotted, and double. Shorthand border: 4px solid #2563eb is the everyday form. Individual longhands help when only one side differs.
topics.whenToUse: Outlining components, inputs, and separators.
topics.whenNotToUse: Focus indication that must not affect layout — outline is often better.
commonMistakes: Setting border: 1px #000 without a style keyword.
beginnerTips: No style means no border even if width and color are set.
topics.title: Border width, style, color

topics.description: border-radius rounds corners. One value rounds all corners; two-to-four values set corners individually. Large radii or 50% on a square create pills and circles. Radius clips the background but does not round the layout box for hit-testing in older mental models — still fine for most UI.
topics.whenToUse: Cards, buttons, avatars, and softer UI chrome.
topics.whenNotToUse: Tiny radii on everything without a design system — keep a consistent scale.
commonMistakes: Using huge radius on short rectangles and getting odd capsule shapes by accident.
beginnerTips: Equal width/height + border-radius: 50% makes a circle.
topics.title: border-radius

topics.description: Side-specific borders (border-left, etc.) create accents and separators without boxing the whole element. Common for list dividers and left accent bars on alerts. You can mix sides freely.
topics.whenToUse: Accents, row separators, and partial outlines.
topics.whenNotToUse: When all four sides share the same border — use the shorthand once.
commonMistakes: Stacking full borders and side borders until the box looks thicker than intended.
beginnerTips: border-bottom on list items plus :last-child { border: 0 } is a classic pattern.
topics.title: Individual borders

topics.summary: Drawn outside the border box; do not take layout space.
topics.description: Outlines draw outside the border and do not take up layout space, so they will not shift neighbors. Excellent for :focus-visible rings. outline-offset adds a gap between the ring and the element. Do not remove focus outlines without a clear replacement.
topics.whenToUse: Focus indicators and temporary debug rings.
topics.whenNotToUse: Permanent decorative frames that should affect layout — use border.
commonMistakes: outline: none with no replacement, trapping keyboard users without a focus cue.
beginnerTips: Prefer :focus-visible for keyboard focus styles users can see.
topics.title: Outlines

topics.description: box-shadow paints one or more shadows: x-offset y-offset blur spread color. Soft, layered shadows suggest elevation for cards and popovers. Shadows do not affect layout size. Prefer subtle shadows so UI does not look muddy.
topics.whenToUse: Cards, dropdowns, modals, and elevated surfaces.
topics.whenNotToUse: Every element on the page — too many shadows flatten hierarchy.
commonMistakes: Huge opaque shadows that look like thick gray borders.
beginnerTips: Separate multiple shadows with commas for layered depth.
topics.title: box-shadow

topics.description: text-shadow adds shadow behind text glyphs. Keep blur and contrast subtle so letters stay sharp. Helpful for light text on busy images; rarely needed on plain body copy.
topics.whenToUse: Display headings over photos or colorful backgrounds.
topics.whenNotToUse: Long paragraphs — shadows reduce clarity.
commonMistakes: Neon multi-colored text shadows that destroy readability.
beginnerTips: A 1px dark halo can improve white text on mixed imagery.
topics.title: text-shadow

topics.description: transition-property lists which properties animate when they change (often on :hover or class toggles). Prefer specific properties like transform and opacity over all — animating layout properties can be janky and expensive.
topics.whenToUse: Smoothing state changes for hover, focus, and UI feedback.
topics.whenNotToUse: Animating large layout reflows (width/top of many items) when transform would do.
commonMistakes: transition: all 1s on complex components, causing sluggish surprises.
beginnerTips: transform and opacity are the safest, smoothest properties to transition.
topics.title: transition-property

topics.description: transition-duration sets how long the animation takes. UI hovers often feel right around 150–300ms. Longer durations suit larger motions; too long makes the interface feel sluggish.
topics.whenToUse: Controlling how snappy or leisurely a transition feels.
topics.whenNotToUse: Critical instant feedback (some toggles should snap).
commonMistakes: Multi-second hover transitions that block feeling responsive.
beginnerTips: Match duration to distance: small color fades can be shorter than big moves.
topics.title: transition-duration

topics.description: Timing functions control acceleration: ease, linear, ease-in-out, or custom cubic-bezier(). ease-in-out feels natural for many UI moves; linear suits continuous spinners. The curve matters as much as duration for perceived quality.
topics.whenToUse: Shaping how a transition speeds up and slows down.
topics.whenNotToUse: When a linear progress feel is required — use linear explicitly.
commonMistakes: Using ease-in for entrances that should decelerate into place (often ease-out feels better).
beginnerTips: DevTools has a curve editor for cubic-bezier experiments.
topics.title: transition-timing-function

topics.description: transition-delay waits before the transition starts. Useful for staggered sequences or avoiding accidental hover flashes. Keep delays short so the UI does not feel laggy.
topics.whenToUse: Staggered reveals and preventing hyper-sensitive hover flicker.
topics.whenNotToUse: Primary button feedback that should feel immediate.
commonMistakes: Long delays that make the interface feel broken or unresponsive.
beginnerTips: Stagger children with increasing delays (0ms, 50ms, 100ms).
topics.title: transition-delay

topics.description: Pair :hover (and focus-visible) with short transitions for polish: lift cards, darken buttons, fade borders. Keep motion small and fast. Always provide an equivalent focus style for keyboard users.
topics.whenToUse: Interactive polish on cards, buttons, and links.
topics.whenNotToUse: Decorative motion that distracts from reading or slows every hover.
commonMistakes: Hover-only cues with no :focus-visible style for keyboard users.
beginnerTips: Transition transform/box-shadow rather than top/margin for smoother lifts.
topics.title: Hover transitions

topics.description: @keyframes defines a named sequence with from/to or percentage waypoints. Reuse the name with the animation property on any element. Keep keyframes focused on transform and opacity when you can for smoother results.
topics.whenToUse: Repeating or multi-step motion beyond a simple A→B transition.
topics.whenNotToUse: One-off hover color changes — a transition is simpler.
commonMistakes: Animating left/top for motion that transform: translate could handle more smoothly.
beginnerTips: Name keyframes by intent (pulse, spin, fade-in), not by element.
topics.title: @keyframes

topics.description: animation-name links an element to a @keyframes rule. Without a duration (or shorthand), you may not see motion. The shorthand animation property sets name, duration, timing, iteration, and more in one line.
topics.whenToUse: Connecting elements to defined keyframe sequences.
topics.whenNotToUse: When you have not defined matching @keyframes — the name will do nothing.
commonMistakes: Setting animation-name without duration or iteration and seeing a single freeze frame.
beginnerTips: Typos in the name silently fail — check spelling against @keyframes.
topics.title: animation-name

topics.description: animation-duration is the length of one cycle. Required for visible motion in practice. Shorter feels snappier; loaders often sit around 0.6–1.5s per loop. Duration interacts with timing function for feel.
topics.whenToUse: Tuning how long each animation cycle takes.
topics.whenNotToUse: Zero-duration experiments left in production by mistake.
commonMistakes: Extremely slow infinite animations that distract from content.
beginnerTips: Match spinner duration to how “busy” the wait should feel.
topics.title: animation-duration

topics.description: animation-delay waits before the first cycle starts. Stagger multiple elements for cascading entrances. Combined with fill-mode, delayed animations can hold starting or ending styles cleanly.
topics.whenToUse: Staggered entrance animations and sequenced motion.
topics.whenNotToUse: Feedback that should start immediately on click.
commonMistakes: Long delays that make users think the UI stalled.
beginnerTips: Use both fill-mode with delay so the element stays invisible until it starts.
topics.title: animation-delay

topics.summary: How many cycles — number or infinite.
topics.description: iteration-count sets how many times the sequence runs — a number or infinite. Pair with alternate for ping-pong motion. Finite counts are better for entrance effects; infinite suits loaders (respect reduced-motion preferences).
topics.whenToUse: Loaders (infinite) or short repeating emphasis (finite counts).
topics.whenNotToUse: Infinite motion on large content areas that users must read.
commonMistakes: Endless bouncing on marketing heroes that never settles.
beginnerTips: Offer a prefers-reduced-motion alternative that cuts infinite animation.
topics.title: animation-iteration-count

topics.description: animation-direction controls playback: normal, reverse, alternate, and alternate-reverse. alternate plays forward then backward, perfect for pulsing without writing mirrored keyframes.
topics.whenToUse: Ping-pong motion and reversing a sequence without new keyframes.
topics.whenNotToUse: One-shot entrances that should only run forward once.
commonMistakes: Expecting reverse to flip transform origins in complex ways — test visually.
beginnerTips: alternate + infinite is a common breathe/pulse pattern.
topics.title: animation-direction

topics.description: fill-mode controls whether keyframe styles apply before/after the animation runs. forwards keeps the final keyframe state; backwards applies the first keyframe during delay; both does both. Without fill-mode, elements often snap back when the animation ends.
topics.whenToUse: Entrance animations that should stay at the end state.
topics.whenNotToUse: Loops where ending at the final frame would jump — usually none/backwards as needed.
commonMistakes: Wondering why the element snaps back — missing forwards/both.
beginnerTips: both is a safe default for delayed fade-ins.
topics.title: animation-fill-mode

topics.summary: Same idea as transition timing curves.
topics.description: Animation timing functions use the same curves as transitions. steps() creates frame-like motion useful for sprite sheets. Choose ease for organic UI motion and linear for constant-speed spinners.
topics.whenToUse: Controlling acceleration or stepped frame animation.
topics.whenNotToUse: When the default ease already looks fine — do not over-tune.
commonMistakes: Using steps on smooth fades, making opacity look stuttery.
beginnerTips: steps(4) jumps through four holds — great for pixel-style motion.
topics.title: animation-timing-function

topics.summary: When a pointer is over the element.
topics.description: :hover styles an element while a pointing device is over it. Pair with :focus-visible so keyboard users get an equivalent cue. On touch devices hover can be sticky or absent — do not hide essential UI only behind hover.
topics.whenToUse: Pointer affordances on buttons, links, and cards.
topics.whenNotToUse: Essential content or controls that have no non-hover way to appear.
commonMistakes: Relying on hover-only dropdowns that fail on touch keyboards.
beginnerTips: Mirror important hover styles with :focus-visible.
topics.title: :hover

topics.summary: While the element is being activated (clicked).
topics.description: :active applies while the element is being activated (mouse down / tap). Short pressed states give tactile feedback on buttons. Keep the change subtle — scale or darken slightly.
topics.whenToUse: Pressed-state feedback on buttons and clickable controls.
topics.whenNotToUse: Long-lived styles — :active only lasts during activation.
commonMistakes: Huge :active transforms that make clicking feel unstable.
beginnerTips: Combine with transition for a quick press animation.
topics.title: :active

topics.description: :focus matches when an element has focus (keyboard, click, or script). :focus-visible is often better for showing rings only when keyboard navigation needs them. Never remove focus styles without a clear replacement.
topics.whenToUse: Focus indicators on inputs, buttons, and links.
topics.whenNotToUse: outline: none with no accessible replacement.
commonMistakes: Removing outlines site-wide and breaking keyboard accessibility.
beginnerTips: Prefer :focus-visible for custom rings in many modern UIs.
topics.title: :focus

topics.description: :visited styles links the browser knows the user has visited. Privacy rules limit which properties you can change (mostly colors). Do not rely on visited styles for critical information.
topics.whenToUse: Subtle visited link color in content-heavy sites.
topics.whenNotToUse: Complex visited layouts — many properties are blocked for privacy.
commonMistakes: Trying to change visited background images or sizes — browsers block that.
beginnerTips: Keep visited colors distinct but still readable against the page.
topics.title: :visited

topics.description: :checked matches checked radios and checkboxes (and some other states). Combined with sibling combinators, it enables pure-CSS toggles and custom control styling. Still keep native controls accessible.
topics.whenToUse: Styling selected controls and simple CSS-only toggle UI.
topics.whenNotToUse: Complex application state better handled in JavaScript.
commonMistakes: Hiding the real input without providing a keyboard-accessible custom control.
beginnerTips: accent-color is a quick way to theme native checkboxes.
topics.title: :checked

topics.description: :disabled matches disabled form controls. Style a muted look consistently and keep text readable. Disabled controls are not focusable — explain why in UI copy if users need a path forward.
topics.whenToUse: Visually marking unavailable form actions and inputs.
topics.whenNotToUse: Temporarily hiding features users might still need — consider readonly or helper text.
commonMistakes: Low-contrast disabled text that looks broken rather than intentionally inactive.
beginnerTips: Pair disabled styles with cursor: not-allowed when it helps.
topics.title: :disabled

topics.summary: Element that is the first child of its parent.
topics.description: :first-child matches an element that is the first child of its parent. It fails if a different element type comes first. For “first paragraph” regardless of earlier siblings of other types, consider :first-of-type.
topics.whenToUse: Styling the first item in lists and stacks.
topics.whenNotToUse: When you mean the first of a type, not the first child overall.
commonMistakes: Confusing :first-child with :first-of-type.
beginnerTips: If it never matches, inspect whether another node is actually the first child.
topics.title: :first-child

topics.description: :last-child matches the last child of its parent. Classic pattern: borders between items, then remove the border on the last child. Same caveats as :first-child regarding what “last” means.
topics.whenToUse: Removing trailing dividers and special-casing the final item.
topics.whenNotToUse: When gap can replace divider borders entirely.
commonMistakes: Selecting :last-child on the wrong level of nesting.
beginnerTips: Prefer gap when you can avoid border + last-child cleanup.
topics.title: :last-child

topics.description: :nth-child() selects children by pattern: odd, even, or formulas like 3n+1. Powerful for zebra striping and repeating rhythms. Count includes all children, not only matching tag types — use :nth-of-type when that matters.
topics.whenToUse: Zebra tables/lists and patterned repetition.
topics.whenNotToUse: One-off exceptions better handled with a class.
commonMistakes: Using :nth-child when mixed sibling tags shift the count unexpectedly.
beginnerTips: odd/even are the readable forms of 2n+1 and 2n.
topics.title: :nth-child()

topics.description: :not() excludes matches: li:not(.active) styles list items without the active class. Modern browsers allow more complex arguments. Useful for defaults that should skip a special case.
topics.whenToUse: Applying a rule to almost everything except a known exception.
topics.whenNotToUse: Deeply nested :not() chains that become hard to reason about.
commonMistakes: Overusing :not() when a positive class on the targets would be clearer.
beginnerTips: Style the default, then exclude the special case with :not(.special).
topics.title: :not()

topics.summary: Inserts a fictional first child you can style.
topics.description: ::before creates a fictional first child you can style. It requires a content property (even content: ""). Great for icons and decorative labels, but real text content usually belongs in HTML for accessibility.
topics.whenToUse: Decorative markers, icons, and pure CSS ornaments.
topics.whenNotToUse: Important text that screen readers or translators must see in HTML.
commonMistakes: Putting critical messages only in ::before content.
beginnerTips: content: "" is valid when you only need a shaped decorative box.
topics.title: ::before

topics.description: ::after inserts a fictional last child, also requiring content. Common for external-link cues, clearfix hacks (legacy), and decorative endings. Same accessibility caution as ::before: prefer real markup for meaningful content.
topics.whenToUse: Trailing decorative cues and CSS-only adornments.
topics.whenNotToUse: Meaningful suffixes that belong in the document text.
commonMistakes: Relying on ::after for required UI labels.
beginnerTips: Use aria-hidden techniques carefully if decorative icons are added via CSS.
topics.title: ::after

topics.summary: Styles the first letter of a block.
topics.description: ::first-letter styles the first letter of a block container — classic drop caps. Only certain properties apply. Punctuation may be included with the letter depending on the browser and content.
topics.whenToUse: Editorial drop caps and decorative article intros.
topics.whenNotToUse: UI chrome and forms — it is a long-form typography tool.

files.code: Drop cap styling makes the first letter stand out.

commonMistakes: Applying ::first-letter on inline elements where it has no effect.
beginnerTips: Float + larger font-size is the usual drop-cap pattern.
topics.title: ::first-letter

topics.description: ::first-line styles the first formatted line of a block as it wraps. Allowed properties are limited (color, font, etc.). The “first line” changes as the container width changes.
topics.whenToUse: Subtle emphasis on the opening line of a paragraph.
topics.whenNotToUse: Precise word-level styling — wrapping makes the target unstable.

files.code: The first line receives special styling while the rest of this paragraph remains normal as it wraps.

commonMistakes: Expecting margin/padding properties that ::first-line does not support.
beginnerTips: Resize the container to see the styled line change.
topics.title: ::first-line

topics.description: ::selection styles the highlighted text selection. Keep contrast strong so selected text stays readable. Browser support is good for basic color/background; do not rely on exotic properties.
topics.whenToUse: Brand-aligned selection colors with solid contrast.
topics.whenNotToUse: Low-contrast selections that make copying text hard.
commonMistakes: Light gray selection on white backgrounds.
beginnerTips: Test selection colors on both light and dark backgrounds if you support both.
topics.title: ::selection

topics.description: Custom properties are variables written as --name: value. They inherit to descendants, so defining tokens on :root themes a whole page. Redefine a variable on a subtree to scope a local theme (e.g. a dark card).
topics.whenToUse: Design tokens: colors, spacing, radii, shared across components.
topics.whenNotToUse: One-off values used a single time with no reuse — a plain value is fine.
commonMistakes: Forgetting var() and writing color: --accent which is invalid.
beginnerTips: Name tokens by role (--color-accent) not only by raw hue (--blue-500) when possible.
topics.title: Custom properties

topics.summary: Reads a custom property with optional fallback.
topics.description: var(--name) reads a custom property. var(--name, fallback) uses the fallback when the variable is invalid or missing. Fallbacks keep components resilient while tokens are still evolving.
topics.whenToUse: Consuming tokens and providing safe defaults.
topics.whenNotToUse: Computed values that need calc without a variable — use calc directly.
